+# Physical widener: related problems that are compute constrained
+
+The root question (framer.md) is judged not compute-bound in its central claim: molecular mapping of capsid–receptor binding is necessary but not sufficient for transcytosis fate, because the decision point is post-binding endosomal sorting. This file widens to *related* problems that do count as compute constrained under three tests: (i) it is still open whether more parallel compute would change the answer; (ii) compute is already known to bind; (iii) the answer is slow because its steps run one after another, even where more hardware would change only how soon it arrives, not the answer itself.
+
+---
+
+## Option 1: Exhaustive capsid–receptor complex enumeration (docking and AlphaFold-Multimer)
+
+**Summary.** Enumerate binding modes of engineered capsid libraries against the BBB receptor panel (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, LRP6, CA4, AAVR) with docking, MD refinement, and AlphaFold-Multimer, then ask whether transcytosis-competent pairs share a geometric or energetic motif — for example 3-fold-axis engagement of GPI-anchored receptors (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf). Published modeling covers only a handful of complexes: AlphaFold-Multimer models of LRP6 YWTD domain 1 with the AAV-X1 and AAV.CAP-Mac VR-VIII peptides, built with AlphaFold-Multimer-v3 via ColabFold v2.3.5 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518), and an AlphaFold model of the VCAP-102 capsid with ALPL (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf) — against an experimental catalog of ~150 high-resolution AAV capsid structures, more than 50% determined in the last 5 years (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079).
+
+**Root link.** Bears on Q3 — for which capsid–receptor binding signatures transcytosis occurs — specifically whether a shared interface motif marks transcytosis-competent complexes.
+
+**Compute_open (open kind).** More parallel compute would buy model runs (capsid × receptor × pose); published measurements of its effect stop at single-digit numbers of AAV–receptor complexes modeled per study — two LRP6 peptide complexes in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518 — and above that it is unknown whether exhaustive enumeration would surface a shared transcytosis-competent motif or demonstrate that no such motif exists.
+
+**Sequential.** none: every capsid–receptor pair is an independent docking or AlphaFold-Multimer job with its own random seeds, so the work already splits into independent pieces.
+
+**Narrowing.** This leaves aside everything after binding — endosomal sorting, lysosomal degradation, nuclear import — so the computed interface geometry stands in for the binding step alone, not for fate. Its answer still moves the root question because it either widens or closes the catalog of candidate signatures (Q3) against which the sufficiency claim (Q1) has to be tested.
+
+**Sources.** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518; https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079
+
+---
+
+## Option 2: Microsecond molecular dynamics of capsid–receptor–membrane assemblies
+
+**Summary.** Run long MD of a capsid plus receptor in a membrane at endosomal pH to watch binding poses, pH-triggered release, and raft/curvature effects: VCAP-102 binds ALPL at Kd ~20 nM at pH 7.4 but dissociates rapidly at pH 5.5 (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf), and AAV9 remains galactose-attached at pH 5.5 (https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00843-21). Coarse-grained Martini3 simulations of AAV2 with AAVR in a model plasma membrane reached microsecond frames and observed AAVR PKD1/PKD2 contacts lasting only ~1 µs at a time (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248).
+
+**Root link.** Bears on Q1/Q3 — whether fate-relevant physics (pH-dependent release, membrane-domain partitioning) is already visible at the binding step, and so whether "molecular mapping" can be pushed toward a trafficking signature.
+
+**Compute_open (settled kind).** settled: longer trajectories are already known to reveal more of the binding configurational space — the AAV2–AAVR coarse-grained study reports that once the capsid is membrane-bound its translational and rotational motion is restricted and "much longer simulation times" would be required to observe how the capsid moves on the membrane (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248).
+
+**Sequential.** One answer waits on a chain of ~2 fs integration steps (the timestep used in the AAV2–AAVR protocol, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248), each step consuming the previous step's forces and coordinates, so one 100 ns run is ~5×10^7 sequential steps and a 1 µs run ~5×10^8; the answer needs several independent replicas (the AAV2–AAVR study reports multiple, its Figures S17–S25 and S28), and a single replica is a one-GPU job that keeps that GPU essentially fully busy (GPU offloading in gmx mdrun, https://manual.gromacs.org/documentation/current/user-guide/mdrun-performance.html). The steps must run in order inside one trajectory, but independent replicas can run at once, and recasting the answer as an ensemble of many short trajectories combined by Markov-state analysis would let them run simultaneously — a payoff only if the capsid–receptor dynamics is metastable so short runs recombine; the nearest source that has tried this is virus-capsid self-assembly MSMs built from many relatively short unbiased trajectories run in parallel (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1402.1784).
+
+**Narrowing.** This leaves aside the cell's sorting machinery — retromer/SNX tubule engagement, lysosomal routing — and treats simulated binding/unbinding and membrane partitioning as a stand-in for the trafficking decision. Its answer still moves the root question by testing whether any fate-relevant physics is recoverable from the binding step at all, which is exactly the sufficiency issue Q1 raises.
+
+**Sources.** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492248; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1402.1784; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf
+
+---
+
+## Option 3: Supervised sequence-to-transcytosis phenotype models
+
+**Summary.** Train sequence-to-function models on paired (capsid features, transcytosis phenotype) data to rank variants for validation. Precedents: deep models predicting AAV2 packaging viability trained on 201,426 assayed variants yielding 110,689 viable capsids (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-00793-4), and Fit4Function's six sequence-to-function models trained on libraries sized at 240K variants or less, which predicted macaque biodistribution from mouse in vivo and human in vitro data (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966).
+
+**Root link.** Bears on Q2 — assigning each variant a fate — and on whether the binding-to-fate gap in Q1 can be closed statistically instead of mechanistically.
+
+**Compute_open (open kind).** More parallel compute would buy model runs (seeds and architectures) and model size; published measurements of its effect stop at ensembles of three architectures (logistic regression, CNN, RNN) over ~2×10^5 labeled variants (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-00793-4) and six Fit4Function models over ≤240K-variant libraries (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966), and above that it is unknown whether more parameters, seeds, or training compute improve transcytosis prediction or whether labeled transcytosis data, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint.
+
+**Sequential.** One training run is a chain of roughly 10^4–10^5 gradient updates, each update waiting on the previous weights' loss, so a converged answer needs multiple independent seeds and, for multi-trait prediction, one model per trait (Fit4Function trained six, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966); a single run is small enough to keep one GPU busy throughout. Within a run the updates must run in order, but different seeds and per-trait models can train at the same time — which pays off when each model fits one GPU and the labeled set is fully visible to every run, the arrangement used by Fit4Function's RNN/LSTM sequence models (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966).
+
+**Narrowing.** This leaves aside the mechanism of the sorting decision and treats a predicted transcytosis score as a stand-in for measured transwell/in vivo fate. Its answer still moves the root question because a predictor that generalizes would show which feature set carries fate information — i.e., how far Q3's signatures can be pushed toward Q1's sufficiency claim.
+
+**Sources.** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-00793-4; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11297966
+
+---
+
+## Option 4: Cryo-EM reconstruction of capsid–receptor complexes
+
+**Summary.** Determine single-particle cryo-EM structures of capsid–receptor complexes — as done for AAV2–AAVR (PKD2) at 2.4 Å (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6561701) — to extend the ~150-structure AAV capsid library (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079) with receptor-bound interfaces; all high-resolution cryo-EM structures of capsid complexes are single-particle reconstructions averaging large numbers of homogeneous particles (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079).
+
+**Root link.** Bears on the interface-mapping component of Q1 (which capsid residues and receptor domains contact) that feeds Q3's signatures.
+
+**Compute_open (settled kind).** settled: map resolution is already known to improve as more particles contribute — in the AAV structural atlas, genome-containing AAV7/11/12/13 reconstructions reached slightly lower resolution than the empty capsids specifically because fewer capsids were used in those reconstructions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7828300).
+
+**Sequential.** One map waits on a chain of processing stages — motion correction, CTF estimation, particle picking, 2D classification, 3D refinement — roughly a dozen sequential stages, each consuming the previous stage's particle stack; the answer needs one reconstruction per complex plus re-runs for empty/full or symmetry-broken states (the AAV2 Rep–capsid work produced separate pentameric and hexameric maps, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713660), and a single refinement keeps one GPU busy for hours to days. The stages must run in order, but the per-particle work inside a stage can run simultaneously — as in the AAV2 Rep–capsid study, where local refinements of 45,150 and 75,559 symmetry-expanded particles ran on GPU computing resources (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713660) — which pays off when a dataset holds tens of thousands of independent particles.
+
+**Narrowing.** This leaves aside affinity, kinetics, and post-binding sorting, so the static interface stands in for the whole binding event. Its answer still moves the root question because residue-level contact maps are the raw material from which any binding signature (Q3) is defined.
+
+**Sources.** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7828300; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713660; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12682079
+
+---
+
+## Option 5: Cross-species receptor–capsid compatibility scoring
+
+**Summary.** Score capsid interfaces against receptor orthologs (ALPL, LRP6, AAVR, and the mouse-restricted LY6A/LY6C1) to predict which signatures translate to humans. Precedents: AlphaFold modeling of VCAP-102–ALPL predicted capsid-contacting ALPL residues conserved across human, cynomolgus macaque, and mouse (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf); LRP6 was picked out as a highly conserved BBB transcytosis receptor via interactome mapping plus AlphaFold-Multimer of capsid–LRP6 complexes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518); and LY6A/LY6C1 lack primate orthologs (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112).
+
+**Root link.** Bears on the species-conditionality caveat of Q3 — whether a binding signature learned in mouse survives in human.
+
+**Compute_open (open kind).** More parallel compute would buy model runs (receptor-ortholog × capsid pairs scored); published measurements of its effect stop at a handful of isoforms — ALPL contact residues compared for one capsid across human, cynomolgus macaque, and mouse (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf) — and above that it is unknown whether exhaustive ortholog scoring would keep, drop, or reorder the GPI-anchored-protein and LRP6 signatures as candidates for human BBB crossing.
+
+**Sequential.** none: each receptor-ortholog × capsid pair is an independent alignment and modeling job, so the work already splits into independent pieces.
+
+**Narrowing.** This leaves aside mouse-only biology (Ly6a polymorphism underlies strain-specific PHP.B tropism, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31696742) and treats interface conservation as a stand-in for actual human transcytosis. Its answer still moves the root question because translatability is a necessary filter on any signature Q3 proposes for human use.
+
+**Sources.** https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.03.12.584703v1.full.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518; https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112

1: # Framing: Can molecular mapping of AAV capsid–receptor interactions on brain microvascular endothelial cells determine transcytosis fate and its binding signatures?
2: 
3: ---
4: 
5: ## 1. Current understanding (relayed before analysis)
6: 
7: ### 1.1 The system
8: 
9: AAV (adeno-associated virus) is the leading in vivo gene-therapy vector; systemic delivery to the CNS requires crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB), whose wall is formed by brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs/BMVECs) with tight junctions and low vesicular density (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7765129; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804). The BBB is not absolutely impermeable to large molecules: multiple proteins cross it by receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT), classically via the transferrin receptor (TfR), insulin receptor, and LDL receptor family (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804). In brain endothelium, caveolae-mediated transcytosis is actively suppressed by Mfsd2a-dependent lipid transport, which keeps BBB transcytosis tightly regulated and low relative to peripheral endothelia (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7765129; https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/4/456).
10: 
11: ### 1.2 AAV variants that cross the BBB vs. those that stay in the endothelium
12: 
13: - **AAV9** crosses the BBB after intravenous administration in rodents, cats, pigs, and non-human primates (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27718541). In primary human BMVEC transwell models, AAV9 penetrates the barrier by an active, cell-mediated process without disrupting TEER or tight-junction markers, and with minimal transduction of the BMVECs themselves (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820). Two-photon imaging shows AAV9 traffics through tubular transport vesicles and accumulates at the basolateral aspect, consistent with transcytosis rather than nuclear import (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820).
14: - **AAV2** does not appreciably cross the BBB; it is endocytosed by BMVECs and trafficked to the nucleus, transducing the endothelium with little transcytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519).
15: - **AAV-PHP.B / PHP.eB** (AAV9-derived, 7-mer insert in VR-VIII) cross the mouse BBB with ~40–60-fold greater brain transduction than AAV9, but this is restricted to mouse strains expressing membrane-localized **LY6A (SCA-1)** and does not translate to primates (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31725765; https://neuroscience.caltech.edu/documents/21479/Sullivan_Abstract_r2022.pdf). LY6A is a GPI-anchored protein; no primate ortholog exists (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf).
16: - **LY6C1**, a related GPI-anchored protein, was identified as a second BBB receptor for engineered AAV capsids; de novo capsid–receptor targeting to LY6A or LY6C1 yields potent vectors with predictable tropisms (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112).
17: - **VCAP-102** (an AAV9 variant with a 6-aa insert in VR-IV, selected by TRACER) shows 20–400-fold increased brain gene transfer in rodents and primates and uses **ALPL** (tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase) as its primary receptor; direct binding of VCAP-102 to human ALPL initiates receptor-mediated transcytosis in a cell-barrier model (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250; https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/05/15/3082003/36461/en/voyager-demonstrates-alpl-receptor-mediated-blood-brain-barrier-transport-of-novel-aav-capsids-in-molecular-therapy-publication.html). ALPL is a GPI-anchored protein, as are LY6A, LY6C1, and CA4 (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf).
18: - **AAV9-X1.1 / AAV-X1 family** shows endothelial-specific tropism in mice that shifts to enhanced neuronal tropism (i.e., transcytosis) in macaque; **LRP6** was identified as a BBB transcytosis receptor for these capsids, a highly conserved target with human-relevant binding sites (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-52149-0; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-38582-7). AAV-BI30 also binds LRP6-E1E2 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
19: - **BR1** (an AAV2 variant with an NRGTEWD insert) transduces BMVECs with little transcytosis, whereas a single Q→N substitution at position 587 (BR1N) confers strong BBB penetration; BR1 and BR1N likely use the same receptor, yet one residue profoundly changes fate (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519).
20: 
21: ### 1.3 Receptor and entry biology
22: 
23: - **AAVR (KIAA0319L)** is the universal proteinaceous AAV entry receptor for most serotypes; it rapidly endocytoses from the plasma membrane and traffics to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4962915; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26814968). Glycans (heparan sulfate for AAV2; sialic acid for AAV1/4/5; terminal galactose for AAV9) act as attachment factors rather than entry receptors (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0966842X2100216X; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21330365; https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12).
24: - AAV9 binds terminal N-linked galactose via a pocket (N470, D271, N272, Y446, W503) at the base of the 3-fold protrusions (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12). Cryo-EM at endosomal pHs shows AAV9 remains galactose-attached at pH 5.5, which may matter for sorting during trafficking (https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/jvi.00843-21).
25: - AAVR itself is not a simple plasma-membrane receptor: cell-surface attachment is AAVR-independent in some contexts, and AAVR acts as a retromer cargo driving endosome-to-TGN transport (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13483459; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391). Even in AAVR-knockout cells, AAV genomes can be detected, indicating a post-attachment trafficking role (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205). An alternate receptor AAVR2 (carboxypeptidase D) enables AAVR-independent transduction of clade E AAVs (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/9J6Z).
26: - Cryo-EM and crosslinking-MS have solved AAV2–AAVR (PKD2) at 2.4 Å (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6561701), AAV1–AAVR and AAV5–AAVR complexes showing divergent binding modes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6704107), and the PHP.eB capsid structure at 2.24 Å showing that the engineered 7-mer loop conformation dictates AAVR (PKD2) binding strength and LY6A-binding availability (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559). A library of ~150 high-resolution AAV cryo-EM structures now exists (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2329050125002244).
27: 
28: ### 1.4 Post-binding steps determine fate
29: 
30: Transcytosis across BBB endothelium requires: (1) luminal binding, (2) endocytosis (clathrin, caveolae, or macropinocytosis), (3) sorting away from late endosome/lysosome degradation toward a transcytotic route, (4) trafficking to the abluminal membrane, and (5) exocytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067). Classic RMT biology shows that binding alone does not set the itinerary: high-affinity or bivalent anti-TfR antibodies are sorted to lysosomes, whereas monovalent or low-affinity binders are sorted to transcytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29877588). For AAV specifically, AAV5 transcytosis uses an entry pathway independent of its transduction pathway (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16368273), and inhibiting transcytosis increases intracellular vector and transduction, demonstrating that transcytosis and transduction are competing fates (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16368273; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205). The BR1/BR1N comparison is the cleanest AAV demonstration that receptor binding alone does not determine the in vivo outcome (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519). More generally, "receptor binding alone does not fully explain AAV tissue tropism in vivo" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12926770).
31: 
32: ### 1.5 Computational tools in play
33: 
34: Machine learning has been applied to AAV capsid design for viability/packaging and tropism (https://arep.med.harvard.edu/pdf/Bryant_Kelsic_ML_2021.pdf; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349), including multi-objective models predicting liver tropism and manufacturability across species (https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240809/Machine-learning-revolutionizes-gene-delivery.aspx) and prescreening of production-fitness for library design (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Cox.pdf). AlphaFold-Multimer has been used to model capsid–receptor complexes (e.g., VCAP-102–ALPL; LRP6–X1/CAP-Mac) (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. Predictions (made before deep analysis)
39: 
40: **P1.** Molecular mapping of capsid–receptor binding on BMECs will be **necessary but not sufficient** to classify variants as transcytosing vs. intracellularly retained. Binding identity and interface structure constrain fate but do not determine it, because the decision point is intracellular sorting, not surface engagement.
41: 
42: **P2.** A **receptor-class signature** will correlate with transcytosis: engagement of GPI-anchored proteins (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, CA4) will associate with BBB crossing more strongly than engagement of AAVR or HSPG/glycan attachment factors, because GPI-APs reside in lipid-raft/caveolar domains implicated in transcytotic transport.
43: 
44: **P3.** That correlation will have **known exceptions** (BR1 vs. BR1N with the same receptor; AAV2 vs. BR1 both BMVEC-tropic with different fates), proving that binding signatures underdetermine outcome.
45: 
46: **P4.** No purely structural/biophysical signature (contact residues, Kd, stoichiometry) will be found that is both necessary and sufficient for transcytosis across species; the missing variable is the capsid/receptor's post-endocytic sorting behavior.
47: 
48: **P5.** The problem as posed will therefore **not be compute-bound**: the decisive evidence is mechanistic and empirical (trafficking assays, single-amino-acid counterexamples), not a matter of insufficient computation. Compute can expand the catalog of binding signatures but cannot close the causal gap from binding to transcytosis.
49: 
50: ---
51: 
52: ## 3. Problem definition (before answering)
53: 
54: ### 3.1 What exactly is being asked
55: 
56: The question contains three nested sub-questions:
57: 
58: - **Q1 (sufficiency):** Can *molecular mapping* of capsid–receptor interactions on BMECs *determine* (i.e., predict/classify) which AAV variants transcytose the BBB vs. remain intracellular?
59: - **Q2 (phenotype assignment):** For each variant, which fate does it have?
60: - **Q3 (signature identification):** For which *capsid–receptor binding signatures* does transcytosis occur?
61: 
62: "Molecular mapping" is ambiguous and must be decomposed. It could mean any of:
63: (a) **Interaction discovery**: which receptor does a capsid bind (affinity proteomics, CRISPR screens, SPR/BLI panels);
64: (b) **Interface mapping**: which capsid residues and receptor domains contact (cryo-EM, crosslinking-MS, mutagenesis);
65: (c) **Energetics**: Kd, kon/koff, stoichiometry, pH dependence;
66: (d) **Structural signatures**: loop conformations, insert topologies, glycan-binding pockets.
67: 
68: Each of these characterizes the **binding step only**. Transcytosis fate is an emergent property of the entire pathway: binding → internalization → endosomal sorting → transcytotic trafficking → abluminal exocytosis, competing with lysosomal degradation and nuclear import/transduction of the endothelium (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205).
69: 
70: ### 3.2 The causal chain and where information is lost
71: 
72: ```
73: Capsid + Receptor on BMEC
74:         │  ← molecular mapping lives HERE (Kd, contacts, structure)
75:         ▼
76:    Endocytosis (clathrin / caveolae / macropinocytosis)
77:         ▼
78:    Early endosome sorting station                    ← fate decision lives HERE
79:         ├──► transcytotic tubule/vesicle ──► abluminal exocytosis  = BBB crossing
80:         ├──► late endosome / lysosome                                = degradation
81:         └──► TGN / nucleus (endothelial transduction)                = intracellular retention
82: ```
83: 
84: The mapping information is generated upstream of the sorting decision. Two capsids with identical receptor binding can be sorted differently; conversely, two capsids with different binding modes can converge on the same transcytotic route. Therefore **there is a many-to-one and one-to-many relationship between binding signature and fate**, and no function f(binding_signature) → {transcytose, retain} can be exact without additional variables.
85: 
86: ### 3.3 The decisive empirical counterexample
87: 
88: **BR1 vs. BR1N**: same receptor on BMVECs, one amino acid (Q587N) changes the outcome from endothelial transduction with little transcytosis to robust BBB penetration and neuronal transduction. The authors conclude: "receptor binding alone does not determine the final outcome in vivo" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519). This single result falsifies the strong form of Q1 ("mapping determines fate") unless "molecular mapping" is expanded to include features that encode post-binding behavior (e.g., receptor oligomerization state, membrane-domain partitioning, endocytic motif engagement) — but those are no longer purely "capsid–receptor binding" signatures; they are trafficking signatures.
89: 
90: ### 3.4 The second independent line of evidence: RMT affinity/valency
91: 
92: For TfR-directed antibodies at the BBB, monovalent or lower-affinity binders are sorted to transcytosis while bivalent/high-affinity binders are sorted to lysosomes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29877588). Here the *same receptor* yields opposite fates depending on binding mode (valency, affinity) — i.e., even the binding signature's quantitative parameters are not sufficient; the cell's sorting machinery reads avidity/cluster size. Transcytosis rates were directly proportional to partition into early endosome fractions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5888858).
93: 
94: ### 3.5 What mapping *can* contribute (the partial answer)
95: 
96: 1. **Receptor identity** is strongly informative at the family level:
97:    - GPI-anchored receptor engagement (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL) associates with BBB transcytosis in mouse and, for ALPL, in cross-species/human cell-barrier models (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250).
98:    - LRP6 engagement associates with primate-relevant BBB transcytosis for X1.1-family capsids (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
99:    - AAVR/galactose engagement is compatible with both fates (AAV9 crosses; AAV2 does not; PHP.eB weakens AAVR while gaining LY6A) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820).
100: 2. **Interface geometry/topology**: the PHP.eB 7-mer bent-loop conformation tunes AAVR affinity and LY6A availability (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559); VCAP-102's 6-aa VR-IV insert mediates ALPL binding at the 3-fold axis (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf); AAV9's galactose pocket sits at the base of 3-fold protrusions (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12).
101: 3. **Species conservation of the receptor** is a necessary translatability filter: LY6A/LY6C1 are mouse-specific; ALPL and LRP6 are conserved (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
102: 
103: ### 3.6 What mapping cannot determine without functional assays
104: 
105: - Whether a bound complex is internalized via a transcytosis-competent route (caveolar/lipid-raft vs. clathrin-to-lysosome) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7765129).
106: - Whether the capsid escapes endosomes (PLA2-dependent) toward nuclear import instead of crossing (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391).
107: - Quantitative partition between early-endosome transcytotic tubules and late-endosome/lysosome degradation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5888858).
108: - Species- and strain-specific receptor expression (Ly6a polymorphism underlies strain-specific PHP.B tropism) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31696742).
109: 
110: ### 3.7 Reformulation of the question
111: 
112: Q1 is best answered as: *partially — mapping identifies the receptor-class and interface correlates of transcytosis, but cannot alone determine fate; fate requires a trafficking readout.* Q3 is best answered as: *the strongest available signature is engagement of a GPI-anchored luminal receptor (LY6A/LY6C1/ALPL, and by extension CA4) or of conserved RMT receptors like LRP6, with caveats (same-receptor different-fate cases; species-restricted receptors).*
113: 
114: ---
115: 
116: ## 4. Deep analysis
117: 
118: ### 4.1 Is there a "binding signature" that is predictive?
119: 
120: The literature supports a **probabilistic, class-level signature** rather than a deterministic residue-level one:
121: 
122: - **Signature S1 (GPI-AP engagement):** PHP.B/PHP.eB (LY6A), engineered LY6C1-targeting capsids, VCAP-102 (ALPL). Mechanistic plausibility: GPI-APs partition into lipid rafts and undergo apical-to-basolateral transcytotic delivery in polarized cells (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(19)30054-1), and the Voyager model explicitly groups LY6A, LY6C1, CA4, ALPL as a GPI-AP receptor family for BBB transport (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf).
123: - **Signature S2 (conserved RMT receptor engagement):** LRP6 for AAV9-X1.1/BI30 family (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
124: - **Signature S3 (AAVR engagement strength):** PHP.eB's altered tropism arises from *weakening* AAVR/PKD2 interaction while gaining LY6A — suggesting that reduced AAVR-driven TGN/nuclear routing plus a transcytotic receptor is favorable for crossing (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559).
125: - **Non-signatures:** glycan attachment (galactose for AAV9, HS for AAV2) is compatible with both fates and is not predictive (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21330365).
126: 
127: **Counterexample pressure on all signatures:** BR1/BR1N shows one residue flips fate within a fixed receptor usage (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519); AAV2 and BR1 share BMVEC transduction with little crossing while AAV9 and BR1N cross (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820). Hence no residue-level binding signature is sufficient.
128: 
129: ### 4.2 The species problem
130: 
131: Any signature learned in mouse (LY6A/LY6C1) is not automatically valid in human: LY6A/LY6C1 lack primate orthologs (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112), and PHP.eB failed in NHPs (https://neuroscience.caltech.edu/documents/21479/Sullivan_Abstract_r2022.pdf). Human-relevant signatures must involve conserved receptors (ALPL, LRP6) or conserved expression patterns (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518). This is a biological constraint on the signature space, not a computational one.
132: 
133: ### 4.3 Could compute change this?
134: 
135: Compute enters at:
136: - **(a) Structural enumeration:** docking/MD/AlphaFold-Multimer across capsid libraries × receptor panels to classify binding modes (in the spirit of https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518 and https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf). This expands the *catalog* of S1–S3-like signatures but cannot validate fate.
137: - **(b) ML on paired (binding features, transcytosis phenotype) data:** sequence→function models are feasible for capsid properties (https://arep.med.harvard.edu/pdf/Bryant_Kelsic_ML_2021.pdf; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349), but the label "transcytoses across human BBB" requires experimental transwell/in vivo measurements; the bottleneck is labeled data, not FLOPs.
138: - **(c) Simulating post-binding trafficking** (endosomal sorting, retromer/SNX tubule engagement, GPI-AP raft partitioning) — currently beyond tractable whole-system simulation, and in any case the decisive variables are cell-biological (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804).
139: 
140: **The core answer to Q1 is fixed by mechanistic logic and existing counterexamples (BR1/BR1N; TfR affinity/valency; AAV5 transcytosis independent of transduction pathway).** More parallel compute cannot overturn these; it can only refine the signature catalog (Q3) and prioritize experiments. Therefore the problem is **not compute-bound** in its central claim.
141: 
142: ### 4.4 Where parallel compute *would* materially help (candidate compute signals)
143: 
144: 1. **Exhaustive binding-signature enumeration** across engineered capsid libraries vs. the BBB receptor panel (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, LRP6, CA4, AAVR) via docking/MD/AF-Multimer — could reveal whether transcytosis-competent complexes share a geometric/energetic motif (e.g., 3-fold-axis engagement of GPI-APs) beyond the handful of published structures.
145: 2. **Supervised learning of transcytosis phenotype from (sequence, receptor, structural, biophysical) features**, once paired transwell/in vivo labels exist — could convert class-level correlations into quantitative predictors and rank variants for validation.
146: 3. **Cross-species receptor–capsid compatibility scoring** (comparative structural genomics of receptor orthologs + capsid interface conservation) — could predict translatability of a binding signature from mouse to human, addressing the LY6A-to-ALPL/LRP6 gap.
147: 
148: None of these change the qualitative answer to Q1 ("mapping alone is insufficient"); they change the completeness and precision of Q3 ("for which signatures") and the experimental prioritization. Since the question's headline claim is decided by biology rather than compute, the verdict stands.
149: 
150: ---
151: 
152: ## 5. Synthesis
153: 
154: - **Q1:** No — molecular mapping of capsid–receptor binding on BMECs is necessary but not sufficient to determine transcytosis vs. intracellular retention. The fate decision is made by post-binding endosomal sorting, and the same binding signature can yield either fate (BR1 vs. BR1N; TfR affinity/valency; AAV5 transcytosis independent of transduction pathway).
155: - **Q2:** Phenotype assignment requires functional readouts (transwell transcytosis, in vivo CNS transduction vs. endothelial transduction, endosomal colocalization).
156: - **Q3:** The best-supported binding signatures associated with transcytosis are: (i) engagement of GPI-anchored luminal receptors (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL; CA4 by family extension), (ii) engagement of conserved RMT receptors (LRP6), and (iii) weakened AAVR/TGN-routing combined with a transcytotic receptor. Glycan attachment signatures (galactose, HS) are not predictive. All signatures are probabilistic and species-conditional.
157: 
158: The problem is **NOT COMPUTE-BOUND**: the decisive reasoning is causal/mechanistic and rests on published counterexamples and cell-biological sorting logic; parallel compute refines signature catalogs and prioritizes experiments but cannot establish sufficiency of binding for transcytosis.
159: 
160: ---
161: 
162: VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

### 1.4 Post-binding steps determine fate

Transcytosis across BBB endothelium requires: (1) luminal binding, (2) endocytosis (clathrin, caveolae, or macropinocytosis), (3) sorting away from late endosome/lysosome degradation toward a transcytotic route, (4) trafficking to the abluminal membrane, and (5) exocytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067). Classic RMT biology shows that binding alone does not set the itinerary: high-affinity or bivalent anti-TfR antibodies are sorted to lysosomes, whereas monovalent or low-affinity binders are sorted to transcytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29877588). For AAV specifically, AAV5 transcytosis uses an entry pathway independent of its transduction pathway (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16368273), and inhibiting transcytosis increases intracellular vector and transduction, demonstrating that transcytosis and transduction are competing fates (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16368273; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205). The BR1/BR1N comparison is the cleanest AAV demonstration that receptor binding alone does not determine the in vivo outcome (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519). More generally, "receptor binding alone does not fully explain AAV tissue tropism in vivo" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12926770).

### 1.5 Computational tools in play

Machine learning has been applied to AAV capsid design for viability/packaging and tropism (https://arep.med.harvard.edu/pdf/Bryant_Kelsic_ML_2021.pdf; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349), including multi-objective models predicting liver tropism and manufacturability across species (https://www.news-medical.net/news/20240809/Machine-learning-revolutionizes-gene-delivery.aspx) and prescreening of production-fitness for library design (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Cox.pdf). AlphaFold-Multimer has been used to model capsid–receptor complexes (e.g., VCAP-102–ALPL; LRP6–X1/CAP-Mac) (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).

---

## 2. Predictions (made before deep analysis)

**P1.** Molecular mapping of capsid–receptor binding on BMECs will be **necessary but not sufficient** to classify variants as transcytosing vs. intracellularly retained. Binding identity and interface structure constrain fate but do not determine it, because the decision point is intracellular sorting, not surface engagement.

**P2.** A **receptor-class signature** will correlate with transcytosis: engagement of GPI-anchored proteins (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, CA4) will associate with BBB crossing more strongly than engagement of AAVR or HSPG/glycan attachment factors, because GPI-APs reside in lipid-raft/caveolar domains implicated in transcytotic transport.

**P3.** That correlation will have **known exceptions** (BR1 vs. BR1N with the same receptor; AAV2 vs. BR1 both BMVEC-tropic with different fates), proving that binding signatures underdetermine outcome.

**P4.** No purely structural/biophysical signature (contact residues, Kd, stoichiometry) will be found that is both necessary and sufficient for transcytosis across species; the missing variable is the capsid/receptor's post-endocytic sorting behavior.

**P5.** The problem as posed will therefore **not be compute-bound**: the decisive evidence is mechanistic and empirical (trafficking assays, single-amino-acid counterexamples), not a matter of insufficient computation. Compute can expand the catalog of binding signatures but cannot close the causal gap from binding to transcytosis.

---

## 3. Problem definition (before answering)

### 3.1 What exactly is being asked

The question contains three nested sub-questions:

- **Q1 (sufficiency):** Can *molecular mapping* of capsid–receptor interactions on BMECs *determine* (i.e., predict/classify) which AAV variants transcytose the BBB vs. remain intracellular?
- **Q2 (phenotype assignment):** For each variant, which fate does it have?
- **Q3 (signature identification):** For which *capsid–receptor binding signatures* does transcytosis occur?

"Molecular mapping" is ambiguous and must be decomposed. It could mean any of:
(a) **Interaction discovery**: which receptor does a capsid bind (affinity proteomics, CRISPR screens, SPR/BLI panels);
(b) **Interface mapping**: which capsid residues and receptor domains contact (cryo-EM, crosslinking-MS, mutagenesis);
(c) **Energetics**: Kd, kon/koff, stoichiometry, pH dependence;
(d) **Structural signatures**: loop conformations, insert topologies, glycan-binding pockets.

Each of these characterizes the **binding step only**. Transcytosis fate is an emergent property of the entire pathway: binding → internalization → endosomal sorting → transcytotic trafficking → abluminal exocytosis, competing with lysosomal degradation and nuclear import/transduction of the endothelium (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205).

### 3.2 The causal chain and where information is lost

```
Capsid + Receptor on BMEC
        │  ← molecular mapping lives HERE (Kd, contacts, structure)
        ▼
   Endocytosis (clathrin / caveolae / macropinocytosis)
        ▼
   Early endosome sorting station                    ← fate decision lives HERE
        ├──► transcytotic tubule/vesicle ──► abluminal exocytosis  = BBB crossing
        ├──► late endosome / lysosome                                = degradation
        └──► TGN / nucleus (endothelial transduction)                = intracellular retention
```

The mapping information is generated upstream of the sorting decision. Two capsids with identical receptor binding can be sorted differently; conversely, two capsids with different binding modes can converge on the same transcytotic route. Therefore **there is a many-to-one and one-to-many relationship between binding signature and fate**, and no function f(binding_signature) → {transcytose, retain} can be exact without additional variables.

### 3.3 The decisive empirical counterexample

**BR1 vs. BR1N**: same receptor on BMVECs, one amino acid (Q587N) changes the outcome from endothelial transduction with little transcytosis to robust BBB penetration and neuronal transduction. The authors conclude: "receptor binding alone does not determine the final outcome in vivo" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519). This single result falsifies the strong form of Q1 ("mapping determines fate") unless "molecular mapping" is expanded to include features that encode post-binding behavior (e.g., receptor oligomerization state, membrane-domain partitioning, endocytic motif engagement) — but those are no longer purely "capsid–receptor binding" signatures; they are trafficking signatures.

### 3.4 The second independent line of evidence: RMT affinity/valency

For TfR-directed antibodies at the BBB, monovalent or lower-affinity binders are sorted to transcytosis while bivalent/high-affinity binders are sorted to lysosomes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29877588). Here the *same receptor* yields opposite fates depending on binding mode (valency, affinity) — i.e., even the binding signature's quantitative parameters are not sufficient; the cell's sorting machinery reads avidity/cluster size. Transcytosis rates were directly proportional to partition into early endosome fractions (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5888858).

### 3.5 What mapping *can* contribute (the partial answer)

1. **Receptor identity** is strongly informative at the family level:
   - GPI-anchored receptor engagement (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL) associates with BBB transcytosis in mouse and, for ALPL, in cross-species/human cell-barrier models (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250).
   - LRP6 engagement associates with primate-relevant BBB transcytosis for X1.1-family capsids (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
   - AAVR/galactose engagement is compatible with both fates (AAV9 crosses; AAV2 does not; PHP.eB weakens AAVR while gaining LY6A) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820).
2. **Interface geometry/topology**: the PHP.eB 7-mer bent-loop conformation tunes AAVR affinity and LY6A availability (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559); VCAP-102's 6-aa VR-IV insert mediates ALPL binding at the 3-fold axis (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf); AAV9's galactose pocket sits at the base of 3-fold protrusions (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12).
3. **Species conservation of the receptor** is a necessary translatability filter: LY6A/LY6C1 are mouse-specific; ALPL and LRP6 are conserved (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).

### 3.6 What mapping cannot determine without functional assays

- Whether a bound complex is internalized via a transcytosis-competent route (caveolar/lipid-raft vs. clathrin-to-lysosome) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337067; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7765129).
- Whether the capsid escapes endosomes (PLA2-dependent) toward nuclear import instead of crossing (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391).
- Quantitative partition between early-endosome transcytotic tubules and late-endosome/lysosome degradation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5888858).
- Species- and strain-specific receptor expression (Ly6a polymorphism underlies strain-specific PHP.B tropism) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31696742).

### 3.7 Reformulation of the question

Q1 is best answered as: *partially — mapping identifies the receptor-class and interface correlates of transcytosis, but cannot alone determine fate; fate requires a trafficking readout.* Q3 is best answered as: *the strongest available signature is engagement of a GPI-anchored luminal receptor (LY6A/LY6C1/ALPL, and by extension CA4) or of conserved RMT receptors like LRP6, with caveats (same-receptor different-fate cases; species-restricted receptors).*

---

## 4. Deep analysis

### 4.1 Is there a "binding signature" that is predictive?

The literature supports a **probabilistic, class-level signature** rather than a deterministic residue-level one:

- **Signature S1 (GPI-AP engagement):** PHP.B/PHP.eB (LY6A), engineered LY6C1-targeting capsids, VCAP-102 (ALPL). Mechanistic plausibility: GPI-APs partition into lipid rafts and undergo apical-to-basolateral transcytotic delivery in polarized cells (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(19)30054-1), and the Voyager model explicitly groups LY6A, LY6C1, CA4, ALPL as a GPI-AP receptor family for BBB transport (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf).
- **Signature S2 (conserved RMT receptor engagement):** LRP6 for AAV9-X1.1/BI30 family (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
- **Signature S3 (AAVR engagement strength):** PHP.eB's altered tropism arises from *weakening* AAVR/PKD2 interaction while gaining LY6A — suggesting that reduced AAVR-driven TGN/nuclear routing plus a transcytotic receptor is favorable for crossing (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559).
- **Non-signatures:** glycan attachment (galactose for AAV9, HS for AAV2) is compatible with both fates and is not predictive (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21330365).

**Counterexample pressure on all signatures:** BR1/BR1N shows one residue flips fate within a fixed receptor usage (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519); AAV2 and BR1 share BMVEC transduction with little crossing while AAV9 and BR1N cross (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820). Hence no residue-level binding signature is sufficient.

### 4.2 The species problem

Any signature learned in mouse (LY6A/LY6C1) is not automatically valid in human: LY6A/LY6C1 lack primate orthologs (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112), and PHP.eB failed in NHPs (https://neuroscience.caltech.edu/documents/21479/Sullivan_Abstract_r2022.pdf). Human-relevant signatures must involve conserved receptors (ALPL, LRP6) or conserved expression patterns (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40340250; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518). This is a biological constraint on the signature space, not a computational one.

### 4.3 Could compute change this?

Compute enters at:
- **(a) Structural enumeration:** docking/MD/AlphaFold-Multimer across capsid libraries × receptor panels to classify binding modes (in the spirit of https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518 and https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf). This expands the *catalog* of S1–S3-like signatures but cannot validate fate.
- **(b) ML on paired (binding features, transcytosis phenotype) data:** sequence→function models are feasible for capsid properties (https://arep.med.harvard.edu/pdf/Bryant_Kelsic_ML_2021.pdf; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349), but the label "transcytoses across human BBB" requires experimental transwell/in vivo measurements; the bottleneck is labeled data, not FLOPs.
- **(c) Simulating post-binding trafficking** (endosomal sorting, retromer/SNX tubule engagement, GPI-AP raft partitioning) — currently beyond tractable whole-system simulation, and in any case the decisive variables are cell-biological (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804).

**The core answer to Q1 is fixed by mechanistic logic and existing counterexamples (BR1/BR1N; TfR affinity/valency; AAV5 transcytosis independent of transduction pathway).** More parallel compute cannot overturn these; it can only refine the signature catalog (Q3) and prioritize experiments. Therefore the problem is **not compute-bound** in its central claim.

### 4.4 Where parallel compute *would* materially help (candidate compute signals)

1. **Exhaustive binding-signature enumeration** across engineered capsid libraries vs. the BBB receptor panel (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL, LRP6, CA4, AAVR) via docking/MD/AF-Multimer — could reveal whether transcytosis-competent complexes share a geometric/energetic motif (e.g., 3-fold-axis engagement of GPI-APs) beyond the handful of published structures.
2. **Supervised learning of transcytosis phenotype from (sequence, receptor, structural, biophysical) features**, once paired transwell/in vivo labels exist — could convert class-level correlations into quantitative predictors and rank variants for validation.
3. **Cross-species receptor–capsid compatibility scoring** (comparative structural genomics of receptor orthologs + capsid interface conservation) — could predict translatability of a binding signature from mouse to human, addressing the LY6A-to-ALPL/LRP6 gap.

None of these change the qualitative answer to Q1 ("mapping alone is insufficient"); they change the completeness and precision of Q3 ("for which signatures") and the experimental prioritization. Since the question's headline claim is decided by biology rather than compute, the verdict stands.

---

## 5. Synthesis

- **Q1:** No — molecular mapping of capsid–receptor binding on BMECs is necessary but not sufficient to determine transcytosis vs. intracellular retention. The fate decision is made by post-binding endosomal sorting, and the same binding signature can yield either fate (BR1 vs. BR1N; TfR affinity/valency; AAV5 transcytosis independent of transduction pathway).
- **Q2:** Phenotype assignment requires functional readouts (transwell transcytosis, in vivo CNS transduction vs. endothelial transduction, endosomal colocalization).
- **Q3:** The best-supported binding signatures associated with transcytosis are: (i) engagement of GPI-anchored luminal receptors (LY6A, LY6C1, ALPL; CA4 by family extension), (ii) engagement of conserved RMT receptors (LRP6), and (iii) weakened AAVR/TGN-routing combined with a transcytotic receptor. Glycan attachment signatures (galactose, HS) are not predictive. All signatures are probabilistic and species-conditional.

The problem is **NOT COMPUTE-BOUND**: the decisive reasoning is causal/mechanistic and rests on published counterexamples and cell-biological sorting logic; parallel compute refines signature catalogs and prioritizes experiments but cannot establish sufficiency of binding for transcytosis.

---

VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND
